_comment: Scenario templates: opinionated PRESETS that arrange the sandbox into a recognizable mission, filtered by map/era/needs_carrier. Each carries a recipe preset (applied by the frontend to pre-fill the wizard, editable) and a 'brief' tasking block (appended to the mission briefing by the builder - suggested tasking only, NO forced waypoints). EXCEPTION: a template with "route": "strike" gets a player flight plan (WP1 > IP > TARGET > home) built against the first bb_targets package - the one deliberate opt-out from the no-waypoints rule (see builder.py 'strike route'). These are distinct from the crew-ops templates (backseat_*/rio_fleet_defense) which are handled by dedicated builder branches.

carrier_qual.label: Carrier Qualification (CQ) — Case I/III recovery practice at the boat
brief: === TASKING (suggested) — CARRIER QUALIFICATION ===
The boat is steaming into the wind with the pattern open. This is a CASE I
setup — day, clear, and you start on the deck: overhead break, downwind,
groove, fuel state to Marshal. Currency and traps, no enemy tasking.
Recovery tanker is overhead for your bolters and low-state passes.
Grade yourself: bolter, 1-wire to OK-3.
FOR CASE III — the night marshal stack, the push on time, the descent gates
and the ball — fly the Case III track in the Library. It is a taught
syllabus with cues and grades, and it needs DCS: Supercarrier.

library.premise: Traps at the boat — Case I pattern work until your boarding rate is where you want it. Calm deck, empty jet, day. The night recovery is a syllabus of its own: see the Case III track.

acls_practice.label: ACLS Practice — Mode I/IA coupled approaches (SuperCarrier)
brief: === TASKING (suggested) — ACLS PRACTICE ===
SuperCarrier boat, Link4 + ACLS radiating (see the Boat Card for channels).
Work the coupled approach:
- Fly to Marshal, set Link4 (F/A-18: DL20; F-14 RIO enters the freq), ICLS on.
- Commence, needles/ACLS: Mode II (needles, you fly) then Mode I (coupled,
hands-off to touchdown) once you trust the datalink.
Tanker overhead for the go-arounds. Night/weather is set to make it count.
Note: ACLS needs an ACLS-capable hull (SuperCarrier / Stennis) - keep the
carrier on a supercarrier and don't swap to the Forrestal for this one.

library.premise: Mode I/IA coupled approach — fly the needles down to a hands-off night trap in the weather.

cap_alert5.label: CAP / Alert-5 — hold the line, intercept inbound raiders
brief: === TASKING (suggested) — COMBAT AIR PATROL ===
You own a CAP station on the threat axis. AWACS has the picture; check in and
work the intercepts. Enemy CAP is up and probing - expect commit calls.
Tanker on station to keep you on the wall. ROE: your call - this is a training
furball, not a scored engagement. Hold the line, protect the rear, RTB with gas.

library.premise: Hold the line. Sit Alert-5 and scramble to intercept inbound raiders before they cross into friendly airspace.

sead_range.label: SEAD / Wild Weasel Range — work a defended target complex
brief: === TASKING (suggested) — SEAD / WILD WEASEL ===
A defended target area is up ahead - SAM belt around the enemy fields (see the
F10 threat rings and the kneeboard). Roll back the air defenses:
- First on the RWR, sort the emitters, respect the rings.
- HARM/Shrike the acquisition and TR radars; re-attack the shooters.
AWACS has the picture, tanker's behind you. No fixed waypoints - build your own
ingress around the threats. Success = you can fly the target area without a launch.

library.premise: Wild Weasel work over a defended target — bait the SAMs, kill the radars, open the door for the strikers.

berlin_corridor_transit.label: Berlin Corridor Transit — fly the Cold War air corridors to Berlin
brief: === TASKING (suggested) — BERLIN CORRIDOR TRANSIT ===
Three 20-mile-wide corridors run across GDR airspace to West Berlin, ceiling
10,000 ft, all converging on the Berlin Control Zone (see the F10 map — violet
swaths — and the airspace note below). This is an airspace-discipline sortie:
- Pick a corridor (North/Hamburg, Center/Hannover, South/Frankfurt) and hold
inside its lateral limits, below the ceiling, all the way to the Control Zone.
- Straying out over GDR territory is what got you intercepted historically —
the win here is a clean transit, not a fight.
No enemy tasking, no fixed waypoints. Fly the lanes, respect the ceiling, RTB.

(Historical note: the real corridors were open to unarmed transports only — fighters were prohibited. Flying one in an F-4E is a training conceit; the discipline is period-real, your airplane is not.)

library.premise: Thread the real Cold-War air corridors into Berlin — stay in the lane, the whole world is watching.

af_tic_cas.label: Troops in Contact — Ridge-Line CAS (Kandahar A-10)

library.premise: A friendly patrol faces hostile vehicles 800 m away. Check in with a dedicated DCS JTAC on 30 MHz FM, identify the target and provide CAS. No scripted 9-line or automatic danger-close clearance.

brief: == TASKING: TROOPS IN CONTACT ==
A friendly patrol and dedicated Pointer JTAC are placed near the hostile vehicles.
Check in on 30.000 MHz FM using the native DCS JTAC radio menu.
Confirm clearance and friendly positions before release; AWACS is air-picture support, not JTAC.

af_bastion_scramble.label: Bastion Scramble — Harrier Alert (VMA-211)

library.premise: Alert Harrier at Camp Bastion. The QRF needs air NOW — runway alert, first pass counts.

brief: == TASKING: ALERT LAUNCH ==
Immediate launch from Bastion alert. Strike package in the target area.
Fuel is tight - Texaco is airborne if you need it.

af_convoy_overwatch.label: Helmand Convoy Overwatch (F-16 night)

library.premise: A friendly four-truck convoy follows a marked DCS road route after dark. Protect it when two hostile armored vehicles activate near the ambush zone. A notional local overwatch exercise.

brief: == TASKING: CONVOY OVERWATCH ==
The friendly road route and ambush approach area are marked on F10.
A dedicated convoy and proximity-activated hostile ambush are generated.
Use the fitted targeting pod and verify identification before attacking.
This uses the DCS road graph, not a surveyed historical Helmand route.

af_hindu_kush_qra.label: Hindu Kush QRA — Northern Intercept

library.premise: Fast movers pushing south over the Hindu Kush. Scramble from Kandahar, climb hard, and meet them in the high passes.

brief: == TASKING: QUICK REACTION ALERT ==
Overlord holds the picture - expect bandits from the northern fields.
The terrain is the second enemy: MSA in the passes is unforgiving.
Bagram's SAM umbrella is active - respect the rings on the F10 map.

f100_victor_alert.label: Victor Alert — Nuclear QRA (Bitburg F-100D)

library.premise: The Hun's Cold War job: cocked on strip alert, ready to run a low-level strike deep into the SAM belt. Delivery is simulated conventionally — the mission is the profile: low ingress, toss, survive the egress. Notional 1978 DCS adaptation: Bitburg's historical F-100 basing ended in 1961; no nuclear store or automatic toss grading.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): VICTOR ALERT — NUCLEAR QRA ==
You are the alert bird at Bitburg, conventionally armed on wing racks. The klaxon just went.
A designated target sits deep behind the front (DGZ ring on the F10 map).
- Get airborne and go LOW — the SA-2/SA-3 belt owns the medium altitudes.
- Run the corridor on the deck, pop for the toss/LADD delivery, egress low and fast.
No fixed waypoints: pick your own run-in around the threat rings. GCI only — no AWACS.
The whole sortie is about the profile: get in low, deliver, survive the egress.

f100_fulda_cas.label: Fulda Gap CAS — Stop the Armor (Hahn F-100D)

library.premise: A moving armor column advances on a DCS road route. Find it and stop it with guns and unguided bombs. A notional Fulda-inspired exercise.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): BATTLEFIELD CAS — STOP THE ARMOR ==
Red armor is rolling through the target area (F10 + kneeboard). Blunt it.
- Work with guns and the fitted unguided Mk-82s. Identify the moving armor before release.
- Threats are ZSU-23/SA-9 SHORAD class down low: jink, don't loiter, re-attack from a new axis.
No JTAC datalink in this era — talk-on off the F10 picture and your own eyes.
Kill the lead vehicles, break the column's momentum, and get home.

f100_iron_hand.label: Iron Hand — Flak Suppression Escort (Spangdahlem F-100D)

library.premise: Ride shotgun for the strikers — bait the guns, roll in on the SAM sites and flak that come up. The dangerous, low-tech ancestor of Wild Weasel.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): IRON HAND — FLAK SUPPRESSION ==
A defended target complex is ringed with guns and SAMs (threat rings on the F10 map).
- You are the flak-suppression flight: draw the defenses, then roll in on whatever shoots.
- Unguided Mk-82 bombs and the four 20mm on AAA and SAM sites — kill the shooters.
No RWR-cued HARM here: this is eyeballs, the RHAW gear and nerve. Respect the rings.
Success = the strikers get their pass without a launch coming up at them.

f100_sabre_dance_bfm.label: Sabre Dance — Gunfighter BFM (Nevada F-100D)

library.premise: Guns-only day fighter work over the range — learn to fly the Hun on the edge, no missiles, just the pipper and energy.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): GUNFIGHTER BFM ==
A dedicated, clean adversary is up for guns-only BFM. No external missiles on either aircraft.
- This is an energy fight: the Hun bleeds speed in the turn — fly it smart, don't get slow.
- Merge, fight, knock it off, reset. No missiles, no score — just stick-and-rudder.
A practice range is laid on if you want to warm up on strafe first. RTB with gas.

f14_tarps_recon.label: TARPS Recon Run — Photo Pass on a Defended Target (F-14B(U))

library.premise: The Tomcat's other job: run the TARPS camera pod over a defended target and get the imagery out. No shooting — speed, timing and a clean pass are the mission.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): TARPS RECONNAISSANCE ==
You're carrying the recon pod. A target complex needs imagery (F10 + kneeboard).
- Plan a straight, steady run-in across the target for the cameras — wings level, on speed.
- Threat rings are up: time your pass, come in fast, and don't linger for a second look.
AWACS has the picture and a tanker is on the wall. No fixed waypoints — build your run.
Win = a clean photo pass and a live jet on the ramp. Don't trade the airframe for a picture.
TARPS is fitted on exported pylon 6 (physical weapons station 5).
Use the RIO FILM/FRAME controls or Jester Utilities > Air to Ground.
After ending the flight, review Saved Games/DCS_F14/TARPS. No automatic imagery grade.

f14_bombcat_strike.label: Bombcat Precision Strike — Self-Designate a Point Target (F-14B(U))

library.premise: Bombcat. A hardened point target sits inside a SAM ring — lase it yourself and put a LGB through the roof. The multirole Tomcat at its best.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): PRECISION STRIKE ==
A defended point target is marked on the F10 map, ringed by air defenses.
- Ingress around the threat rings, self-designate with the pod and drop LGBs.
- Medium-altitude work above the SHORAD, but the SA belt reaches up — respect it.
AWACS and a tanker are laid on. No fixed waypoints — pick the axis that keeps you alive.
One good pass beats three sloppy ones. Confirm the hit, then egress.

f14_case3_night.label: Case III Night Recovery — Bring It Aboard in the Weather (F-14B(U))

library.premise: The hardest thing in naval aviation: a big-wing Tomcat, a pitching deck, and a black night. Fly the Marshal stack and bring it aboard.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): NIGHT AT THE BOAT ==
Night, weather, the boat below the overcast. This is a currency-and-nerve
sortie and it is a SANDBOX: you start on the deck, and everything after the
launch is yours to set up and fly. Nothing here holds you to the procedure
or grades it. If you do not already know the procedure, learn it in the
Case III track in the Library, which teaches the marshal stack, the push on
time and the descent gates one at a time, with cues and grades, and starts
you airborne in the stack rather than on the deck. It needs DCS: Supercarrier.
Big-wing Tomcat on the ball: fly the deck, keep it on speed, don't chase the
meatball. Recovery tanker is overhead for your bolters and low-state passes.
No enemy tasking. Go again until the traps are where you want them.

cv_alpha_strike_escort.label: Alpha Strike Escort — TARCAP for the Intruders (Forrestal F-14A)

library.premise: The air wing's A-6 Intruders are going downtown. Fly TARCAP off the Forrestal, sanitize the threat axis and keep the MiGs off the strike package.

brief: == TASKING (suggested): ALPHA STRIKE ESCORT (TARCAP) ==
The air wing is launching a medium-attack package — VA-176's A-6 Intruders,
outbound on the threat axis (see the F10 map). You are their fighter cover.
- Launch, sanitize ahead of and around the strike, and hold the CAP between
the Intruders and the enemy fields. Bandits are up — expect commit calls.
- The KA-6D is your gas on the way home (Texaco). AEW has the picture.
No fixed waypoints for you: work the escort geometry off the strike's ingress.
Win = the Intruders get feet-dry and back with no losses to air threats.

gun_belt_strike.label: Gun Belt Strike — routed package attack through the flak (F-4E)

library.premise: A fragged target deep in the gun belt — fly the route, WP1 to IP to TARGET. No SAMs anywhere: every threat ring on the map is guns, and every gun is between you and the aim point.

brief: == TASKING: GUN BELT STRIKE ==
Your flight plan is loaded: WP1 (ingress) > IP > TARGET > home plate. Unusual
for us — this one is fragged, so fly the black line and hit your TOT.
- The target package sits at your TARGET steerpoint (marked on the F10 map).
- There are NO missiles in this war. Every ring on the map is guns: 23mm,
57mm, 100mm. They cannot reach you at altitude — but you cannot hit the
target from altitude either. That trade is the whole mission.
- One pass, haul ass. The second pass is where the gunners have your number.
Off target, egress AWAY from the ring, then direct home plate.

armed_recon_route.label: Armed Reconnaissance — low-level route hunt under the flak (F-5E)

library.premise: Fly the fragged route with eyes out — the briefed target is the anchor, but anything that moves along the way is fair game. Guns only, and the light stuff you never see is the stuff that gets Tigers.

brief: == TASKING: ARMED RECONNAISSANCE ==
Route is loaded: WP1 > IP > TARGET > home. The TARGET package is your
briefed objective; everything along the route is your hunting ground.
- Two Tigers, guns and slick bombs. Nothing on this route out-accelerates you.
- The threat is ALL guns — no launch warnings, no smoke trails. The first
cue you are in a gun ring is tracer. Keep the speed up, never straight
and level below 10,000 ft for more than 20 seconds.
- Log anything you can't kill: convoys, sites, movers. That's the recon half.
Winchester or bingo, direct home.

mig_gun_belt_strike.label: Frontal Aviation Strike — MiG-21 routed attack, guns only (red side)

library.premise: The other cockpit: a MiG-21 with pylons full, a fragged route into NATO's gun line, and a stopwatch. Vulcans and quad-mounts at the target — fast in, one pass, faster out.

brief: == TASKING: FRONTAL AVIATION STRIKE ==
Shturman has your route: WP1 > IP > TARGET > home. Fly it on the clock —
the regiment grades TOT, not style.
- Target package at the TARGET steerpoint. NATO defends it with guns:
Vulcans and 40mm — short-ranged, radar-laid, deadly below 2,000 meters.
- The 21 does one thing well here: speed. Come in fast, put the pipper on,
off in one pass. You have fuel for the route and one attack, not a duel.
RTB direct. A MiG that brings the film home flies again tomorrow.

qf_tanker.label: Tanker Time — air refuelling, starting at the boom
brief: == TANKER TIME ==
You start in the PRE-CONTACT position: 1 nm astern the tanker, 1,000 ft
below the track, already at his speed. No taxi, no climb, no twenty
minutes looking for him on the TACAN.
That is deliberate. Refuelling is thirty seconds of skill wrapped in
half an hour of commuting, and the commuting teaches you nothing. Fly
the last thirty seconds, over and over.
THE REP: close to contact, take fuel, back out to pre-contact, stabilise,
go again. When that gets boring, drop back a mile and re-join from
observation. When THAT gets boring, you can refuel.
The full procedure card — the four positions, the three mistakes, and this
tanker's speed and altitude — is in the briefing and on your kneeboard.
Nothing up here shoots.

library.premise: Start 1 nm astern the tanker, already at his speed. No commute — just the thirty seconds that are actually hard, as many times as you want them.

qf_bfm.label: BFM Merge — one bandit, co-altitude, fight's on
brief: == TASKING: BFM MERGE ==
One adversary, two nautical miles abeam, your altitude. He is looking at you.
- Fight starts at the merge. Energy before angles; check your fuel and
your altitude — the ground has killed more BFM sorties than any bandit.
- Knock it off when someone is dead, defensive at the deck, or bingo.
Re-roll the mission for a different adversary type. Same seed, same bandit.

qf_guns.label: Kill the Guns — airborne on the run-in, AAA-defended target
brief: == TASKING: KILL THE GUNS ==
One target: the vehicle depot marked TGT1 on the F10 map. It defends
itself with gun clusters at the aim point — 23mm up close, heavier out.
- There are NO missiles in this mission. Every ring on the map is guns.
- They can't reach you at altitude; you can't hit anything from altitude.
That trade is the whole sortie. One pass, haul ass.
Winchester or target destroyed: home plate, on the kneeboard.

qf_sam.label: Beat the SAM — airborne just outside the ring
brief: == TASKING: BEAT THE SAM ==
The C2 site marked TGT1 sits inside a SAM ring (threat circles on the F10
map — era-correct systems, so learn THIS threat's timeline).
- Your choice of answer: stand-off outside the ring, run the notch and
trash the shot, or come in under the radar floor on the deck.
- The RWR is the syllabus here. Respect the rings; they are honest.
Target dead or bingo: egress the way you came in, home on the kneeboard.

_by_era: Per-era overrides on top of `recipe`. A template that declares several eras cannot pin one aircraft: the Library offered Carrier Qualification in the Cold War and then handed the engine an F/A-18C. Keys are era -> partial recipe (plus an optional `map` when the default map has no preset for that era).

form_route.label: Formation 1: Route Position — wingman training, no threats
brief: === FORMATION SYLLABUS — STAGE 1 OF 5 ===
You are DASH 2. Lead is a SEPARATE AI aircraft of the same type as
yours, flying a scripted profile that never varies — you cannot build
a sight picture against a leader who improvises.
Lead calls you on the radio when you drift out of position, and once
more when you get back in. One call per excursion, not a running
commentary.
The full instruction sheet is generated for YOUR aircraft and appears
in the mission briefing and on your kneeboard. Read it on the ground.
Written sight-picture references exist for the F-16C, F/A-18C,
F-14A/B/B(U) and F-4E; everything else gets the general principles.
This stage teaches: The position you will actually spend your flying life in. Wide enough to breathe, close enough to be a formation.
Fly it until it is boring, then fly the next stage.

library.premise: Fly Dash 2 on a lead who does nothing at all: straight, level, one speed. You sit in ROUTE — a few hundred feet out, where there is room to breathe. Deliberately boring, because this is the sortie that builds the sight picture everything else stands on.

library.premise: The capstone, and the only one that starts on the ramp. Start up alongside lead, get airborne, rejoin after gear-up, fly the route as a pair and bring it home. This is the sortie a multiplayer server actually asks of you.

bc_tr1.label: B-Course TR-1 — Single-Ship Operations
brief: === B-COURSE TR-1 · SINGLE-SHIP OPERATIONS ===
AETC Syllabus F16C0B00PL (56 FW), Chapter 5, para 5-4. Sortie 1 of 53.
This is the first ride. Nothing is trying to kill you and nothing is
supposed to. The whole sortie is you and the jet.
REQUIRED TASKS (the * items on the real gradesheet):
*2. Instrument departure
*3. Airwork:
a. High and low speed dive recoveries
b. Instrument unusual attitude recoveries
c. Nose-high recovery; horn demonstration
d. Advanced handling: vertical recovery, AOA limiter,
30-degree climb limiter, G-command, slow flight
e. G-AWARENESS EXERCISE / HIGH-G PROFILE — see below
*4. Instrument procedures: non-precision approach, precision approach
*5. VFR patterns and landings: visual straight-in, overhead and closed
patterns, touch-and-go, SIMULATED FLAMEOUT (SFO), full stop
THE G-AWARENESS PROFILE, exactly as the syllabus flies it:
1. Warm-up turn to 4 G.
2. A 180-degree turn at 6 to 8 G.
3. A 180-degree turn at 8 to 9 G.
At least TWO complete AGSM cycles in each of the two hard turns.
In the real course this is monitored on every sortie that sees 5 G or
more, and the AGSM grade gates your solo clearance later.
There is traffic in the pattern at your field. That is deliberate: the
overhead is where you learn to fly the jet and talk at the same time.

library.premise: The first ride of the F-16 B-Course, flown the way Luke flies it. Instrument departure, the full airwork block, the 4G/6-8G/8-9G G-awareness profile, then patterns and an SFO. No threats — the airplane is the syllabus.

bc_ahc.label: B-Course AHC — Advanced Handling Characteristics
brief: === B-COURSE AHC · ADVANCED HANDLING CHARACTERISTICS ===
AETC Syllabus F16C0B00PL (56 FW), Chapter 5, para 5-8.
The bridge sortie between flying the jet and fighting it. You are NOT
here to win a fight — you are here to arrive at his turn circle knowing
where it is.
THE EXERCISE (syllabus task 8b): turn circle entry, run from FIGHT'S ON
through turn circle entry and NO FURTHER. Two setups:
Terminate at entry. Reset. Do it again. The temptation is to press to
the guns; pressing is the next sortie's job.
Also on the card: the offensive radar heat-to-guns exercise (TWO are
desired; the second ends in a reversal to a slow-speed stack), the A-A
switchology drill, and the FENCE check.
THE SECOND SETUP: fly the 9,000 ft exercise until arriving at the turn
circle is boring, then fly the whole card again from the 6,000 ft perch
— 'B-Course AHC (6,000 ft)' in the Library. Same sortie, second half.
Tanker is up: air refuelling is on this card in the real course, and it
is a solo-clearance item.

library.premise: Fight's on to turn-circle entry, then stop. Two setups, 9,000 and 6,000 feet, flown to arrive rather than to win. This is the sortie that makes BFM make sense.

bc_bfm1.label: B-Course BFM-1 — Offensive BFM
brief: === B-COURSE BFM-1 · OFFENSIVE BFM ===
AETC Syllabus F16C0B00PL (56 FW), Chapter 5, para 5-9.
You start at his six with a turn circle to spend. Nine thousand feet is enough room to think and enough rope to hang yourself with an overshoot.
THE SORTIE IS THREE SETUPS, not one:
This card opens at 9,000 ft. The 6,000 and 3,000 ft perches are their own
cards in the Library — 'BFM-1 (6,000 ft)' and 'BFM-1 (3,000 ft)'. Fly all
three; that is the sortie.
Closer is not easier. At 3,000 ft you have a snapshot and a decision;
at 9,000 ft you have a geometry problem. They are different sorties
wearing the same name.
AGSM is a MILESTONE TASK on this sortie in the real course, and it must
grade a '2' before a student is cleared to fly air combat solo.
The standards card for this perch is generated for your aircraft and

f4_turning_phantom.label: Turning the Phantom — keep your speed up, Podner
brief: === TURNING THE PHANTOM ===
TAC ATTACK, Vol 7 No 2, February 1967, page 4. Tactical Air Command
Chief of Safety. Subtitle: 'keep your speed up, Podner'.
WHY THIS SORTIE EXISTS
TAC reviewed 22 F-4 accidents. In ELEVEN of them the aircrew lost
control of the airplane. Line those eleven up and they rhyme:
- TEN were maneuvering — pulling G — when they got into trouble.
- EIGHT were at 300 knots or below. One was between 180 and 200.
- ALL ELEVEN were carrying external stores. Nine had two 370s.
- SEVEN had 12,000 to 14,000 lb of fuel aboard.
- EIGHT were at low altitude — no time or space to recover from a
post-stall gyration.
These were not beginners. Seven of them averaged 175 hours in the
Phantom. That is the uncomfortable part: experience did not save them,
because the airplane was not warning them.
THE THREE THINGS THE ARTICLE WANTS YOU TO FEEL
1. HOW LITTLE G YOU ACTUALLY HAVE DOWN THERE.
Between 250 and 300 knots CAS you have around 3G, plus or minus a
half, before stall. A fighter pilot pulling out of a weapons pass is
used to 4.5 or 5G. Three is not very much, and it does not feel like
a limit until you are through it.
2. WHAT THE STORES DID TO THE STICK.
Category II stability and control tests found external stores cut the
stick force gradient by an average of FIFTY PERCENT. The jet feels
light. Stores also reduce the roll rate that shows up as pre-stall
wing rock — so the airframe's own warning gets quieter exactly when
you need it loudest.
3. WHAT BUFFET IS ACTUALLY TELLING YOU.
Two things at once: you are near critical angle of attack, AND you
have picked up a large amount of drag. Neither helps you turn. Pull
far enough and the drag pulls the speed down — at which point you are
buying turn with airspeed, not with pull. In the article's words: you
end up 'an unmaneuverable sitting duck in free fall trying to regain
what you just threw away.'
FLY IT LIKE THIS
BLOCK 1 — THE 3G DEMONSTRATION. Clean up, get to 250-300 KCAS, and
find the buffet in a level turn. Note the G. Note that it is about 3.
Do it again at 350. That difference is the whole article.
BLOCK 2 — THE DRAG LESSON. From 350, roll into a hard sustained turn
and hold it. Watch the airspeed. Find the moment where pulling harder
stops increasing your turn rate and starts costing you speed. Mark it.
That is your corner, and it is not where you think it is.
BLOCK 3 — THE FIGHT. Line abreast, both hot, and now try to keep 350
KCAS while somebody gives you a reason not to. This is where it stops
being an exercise. The instinct is to trade speed for nose position.
The article is one long argument against that instinct.
THE WARNING YOU MAY NOT GET
The Dash One warns about abrupt entry into accelerated stalls: snatch
the stick back fast enough and you can enter the stall with no
noticeable buffet and no wing rock. All you get is moderate buffet AT
the stall — not before it.
AFT CG, BRIEFLY. The handbook permits external stores until CG reaches
36 percent MAC. A normal range load with standard fuel sequencing sits
around 35.1 percent — under one percent from the limit — and aft CG is
where the light stick and the pitch-up tendency are worst.
THE CONCLUSION, VERBATIM FROM THE ARTICLE'S CLOSE:
'Keep your speed up, Podner, and you won't get into trouble.'
— Don Stuck, McDonnell Field Service Digest
TAC's own summary, one line: in fifty percent of F-4 accidents the
pilot lost control while maneuvering, with stores on, at too low a
speed. Basic maneuvering speed for the F-4 is 350 KCAS. Fly it.

library.premise: February 1967. TAC had lost control of eleven Phantoms out of twenty-two accidents, and the eleven rhymed: maneuvering, stores on, below 300 knots, low. This is that article flown — how little G you really have down there, what the stores did to your stick, and why buffet is not a turn.

aar_1_join.label: Air-to-Air Refuelling 1 (Boom) — Formation on the Tanker
brief: == 1 · THE ANCHOR ==
NEW DEMAND: a stable formation sight picture, held, with no contact objective at all.

is to arrive at the observation position and sit there.

cannot refuel is that they went for contact before they could hold

down, hands steady, without a power change you did not intend. If you
cannot do that, you are not ready to be twenty feet from him.

DROGUE: you fly a probe into a basket that is doing whatever it likes.
Nobody is helping. There is no operator, no director lights, no calls.
THE ONE THING THAT MAKES IT WORK: do not look at the basket. Fly
formation on the TANKER, wide, and let the probe arrive in your
peripheral vision. Every pilot who stares at the basket chases it, and
chasing it is the whole failure mode.

the CUES does.
In daylight you fly the tanker's shape against the sky. At night the
shape is a handful of lights, and depth perception off point sources is
close to nothing. So:
- Use the lit references, not the outline. Fuselage lights, the pod,
the director lights if you have them.
- Trust closure RATE over range. You cannot judge range at night; you
can judge whether something is growing.
- Smaller inputs, earlier. There is no visual cue that will save a
correction you left late.

teach the skill, it removes the crutches.

are carrier airplanes and so are you. The speed and altitude for the one
you actually got are on the procedure card.

aar_boom_0_fit.label: Air-to-Air Refuelling 0 (Boom) — Orientation and Control Check
brief: == 0 · FIT CHECK ==
NEW DEMAND: none. This is the diagnostic. Can you sit next to a
large airplane and stay there, and do your controls do what you
think they do.
There is no plug in this ride and no reason to attempt one.
FIRST, ON THE GROUND OR IN THE CRUISE: check your bindings. The
refuelling door or probe, PTT, speedbrake, trim, and the
disconnect control. Reaching for a control you have not bound
while twenty feet from a tanker is how people hit tankers.
TWENTY SECONDS TO SETTLE. Scoring does not begin the moment you
spawn. If you are in VR, use that window: recenter sitting
naturally with square shoulders, and set seat height so the
tanker reference is visible without a crouch you cannot hold for
ten minutes.
THE THROTTLE DRILL, which is the actual content of this ride.
From a safe in-trail position, repeat this cycle:
1. Close 20-30 feet.
2. STOP the closure without changing your vertical or lateral picture.
3. Drift aft 20-30 feet.
4. Stop the aft drift.
5. Return to the original sight picture.
Three smooth cycles and you are ready for the next ride. Fewer than
three and you are not — which is worth knowing now rather than at the
boom.
PULSE AND COUNTER-PULSE. Find the power setting that produces zero
fore/aft drift; that is your BASELINE. Drifting aft: add a small pulse.
Then — before the closure becomes obvious — take most of it back out.
That second movement is the counter-pulse and it is the part people
skip. Leaving the correction in is what carries you through zero and
into the overshoot.
The goal is not a motionless throttle. It is small, early corrections
around a known baseline. One knot of mismatch is 1.7 feet per second,
so a difference you cannot see becomes an aircraft length in ten.
BOOM LANE NOTE. When you get there, an operator will fly the boom into
your receptacle. That is half the problem solved for you — and it is
exactly why your half has to be still. Your job in contact is to stop
moving, and this ride is where you find out whether you can.
F-16 SPECIFIC: opening the air-refuelling door changes the flight-control
gains. Open it several minutes early if external tanks need to
depressurise, and expect the jet to feel different afterwards. That is
the airplane agreeing that this task wants lower gain.
THIS RIDE IS GRADED. You will be told when you have held position
for fifteen seconds, and again at sixty. If you never hear the
first call, this is exactly the ride you needed — fly it again

timing_1_flythecard.label: Timing 1 — Fly the Card (F-4E)

library.premise: The flight plan has a clock on it for the first time. Wheels up three minutes after the mission starts, then WP1, IP and TARGET each at a printed time. Graded at all four.

brief: == TIMING 1: FLY THE CARD ==
Every leg on your kneeboard now carries groundspeed, leg time,
cumulative time and an ETA. The anchor is TAKEOFF: wheels up three
minutes after the mission clock starts, and everything counts from
there. Nothing else is asked of you on this ride.
- Hack your clock at wheels-up. Fly the briefed speed on each leg.
- The first leg is timed on a climb schedule, not at cruise: if you
level off early or late you will see it at WP1.
- The coach calls EARLY / ON TIME / LATE at WP1, IP and TARGET,
and opens a scorecard a minute after the target.
Base 50. On time +10 a point; late -10; early -5. Fly it twice.

timing_2_hitthetot.label: Timing 2 — Hit the TOT (F-4E)

library.premise: Time on target is fixed at 05:45:00 and the mission clock was solved backwards from it. Thirty seconds either side, and the TOT counts double.

brief: == TIMING 2: HIT THE TOT ==
The anchor is the TOT: 05:45:00 at TARGET, plus or minus thirty
seconds. Read the timing block: the mission clock starts when it
does BECAUSE that time has to be met — wheels up, WP1 and IP are
all derived from the target time, not the other way round.
- Late at WP1 is recoverable: the IP leg has speed in hand.
- Late at the IP is not. The run-in is 76 seconds long.
- Early is the easier problem: a 30-second S-turn before the IP
costs nothing; a 30-second dash after it costs the TOT.
TARGET on time is +20 on this ride; late or early there costs double.

timing_3_thepackage.label: Timing 3 — The Package (F-4E)

library.premise: Two Phantoms fly your card two minutes ahead of you on LOCKED ETAs. Their timeline is real; yours has to fit behind it. Push WP1 at 12:35:00.

brief: == TIMING 3: THE PACKAGE ==
A two-ship of Phantoms flies the same card two minutes ahead of
you, and their ETAs are LOCKED — DCS will fly them to the second.
The anchor is the PUSH: WP1 at 12:35:00, plus or minus a minute.
- The package calls when it crosses the IP. If you are on time,
you are two minutes behind it — outside its frag, inside its
suppression. That spacing IS the mission.
- Do not catch them up. Faster than the card at the IP puts you
over the target while their bombs are still in the air.
- Do not fall back. Two minutes late and the gunners have reloaded.
Wheels-up, WP1 (double), IP and TARGET are all graded.

timing_4_absorbtheearly.label: Timing 4 — Absorb the Early (F-4E)

library.premise: A three-minute hold at WP1, on purpose: you will get there early, and the lesson is pushing at the ETA rather than on arrival. TOT 05:50:00.

brief: == TIMING 4: ABSORB THE EARLY ==
Same anchor as ride 2 — TOT 05:50:00, plus or minus thirty seconds
— but the card carries a three-minute HOLD at WP1. You will reach
WP1 about three minutes before its printed ETA. That is planned.
- Arrive at WP1, turn onto a racetrack (one-minute legs), and
push out of the hold on the WP1 ETA — not when you get there.
- The WP1 grade is taken when you enter the zone, so expect an
EARLY call there. It is the IP and the TARGET that count.
- This is how every professional package absorbs an early takeoff,
a short vector or a tailwind: the hold is the shock absorber.
IP and TARGET on time, after a hold you flew by the clock: that is the pass.

form_precheck.label: Formation 6: Pre-Check — the check profile, coach on
brief: === FORMATION SYLLABUS — PRE-CHECK ===
You are DASH 2 on an AI lead flying the CHECK profile, unchanged.
The coach is still on: lead calls you out of position and back in.
The check-ride engine runs alongside and prints its card at the end,
labelled PRACTICE — items U / F / G / E, overall Q / Q- / U.
The last dual ride before a check flies the check profile. Fly this
until the card says Q, then fly the check.

library.premise: The check ride's exact profile — level, a turn each way, a climb, two speed changes, a descent, then the pitchout and rejoin — with lead still calling you out of position, and the check's own card at the end so you know what it will score.

form_check.label: Formation 7: Check Ride — Fingertip, silent
brief: === FORMATION SYLLABUS — CHECK RIDE ===
You are DASH 2. Lead flies the check profile and says three things:
the brief, the pitchout, and the card. Nothing else.
Grading arms 20 s after you settle in the 60 m band and runs until
the pitchout; then the rejoin is timed. Inside 12 m of lead, lost
for 30 s, or not rejoined in 300 s is a critical item — a U.
Record the card on the gradesheet. An instructor in the other
seat, or watching in multiplayer, grades line, corrections and
radio; alone, grade those yourself against the Standards.

library.premise: The same profile, and nobody talks. Time in the band while lead is level, turning and changing energy; the rejoin on the clock; three critical items. U / F / G / E per item, Q / Q- / U overall. The sim grades what it can see; the gradesheet leaves the wingline and the radio to the IP.

timing_5_check.label: Timing 5 — Check Ride (F-4E)

library.premise: TOT 06:00:00, and nobody talks. Wheels-up, WP1, IP and TARGET graded U / F / G / E on the clock; late at the target is a critical item. Q, Q- or U at the end.

brief: == TIMING 5: CHECK RIDE ==
The anchor is the TOT: 06:00:00 at TARGET. The coach is silent —
one hack at the start, then the card a minute after the target.
- E inside ten seconds of a point's time; G inside its window;
F early; U late or not reached.
- Late at TARGET is a critical item: the check is a U.
- Q needs G or better at every point; an F anywhere is a Q-.
Nobody is surprised on a check ride. If you are, fly rides 2 and 4 again.
